To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

cigarette smoking was associated with cancers of all 10 sites examined in males and 8 sites examined in females; that consumption of alcoholic beverages was associated with cancers in 8 of 12 sites examined in both sexes; that college education and high income were both associated with cancer of 4 sites in males and 6 sites in females; and that these two indicators of high socioeconomic position showed inverse association with cancers of 4 sites examined in females.
the following cancer sites are positively associated with cigarette smoking: oral cavity, larrynx, esophagous, pancreas, lung, stomach, bladder, kidney and uterine cervical cancer.
the lifetime use of cigarettes is positively associated with cancers of 9 specific sites, and that the lifetime use or consumption of alcohol is positively associated with 8 cancer sites.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the role of tobacco and alcohol in the etiology of human cancer, with the role of socioeconomic status in modifying the effects of tobacco and alcohol and in the etiology and prognosis of cancer, and with the role of the environment in modifying the effects and the distribution of cancer.
the etiologic role of smoking, drinking, and other factors in the etiology of cancer.
the role of cigarette smoking, drinking, and socioeconomic factors in the etiology of human cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
tobacco and alcohol consumption, education, and income are all significantly associated with the occurrence of cancer in man.
cigarette smoking is a major cause of lung cancer and that it is probably a major cause of cancers of the oral and nasal cavities, larynx and esophagus, pancreas and stomach, kidney and bladder.
cigarette smoking is a major etiologic factor for cancer of the lung, and a minor factor for cancers of the larynx, lip-tongues, oral cavity, bladder, pancreas, kidney, esophagus and cervix.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the results obtained from this analysis of the Third National Cancer survey are consistent with the hypothesis that tobacco and alcohol consumption are important etiologic agents in the causation of many cancers, and also that socioeconomic status may play a role in the etiology of certain cancers.
the results support the concept that cigarette and tobacco use, and alcohol consumption, are etiologically related to many cancers and that socioeconomic status may modify the effects.
cigarette smoking, alcohol consumption, education, and income are all important factors in cancer etiology and that their effects are not uniform across all sites.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a strong relationship between tobacco and alcohol consumption with cancer.

the associations of cancer with cigarette smoking, alcohol consumption, socioeconomic status, and other variables were not consistent for all sites, and the associations were not the same for males and females.
the association of tobacco with cancer sites is stronger than the association of alcohol with these same sites.
